Valproic Acid / Divalproex Sodium.MOA: Increases GABA levels by inhibiting GABA transaminase; also blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and T-type calcium channels.
ADEs: Teratogenicity (e.g., neural tube defects) (BLACK BOX WARNING)
contraindications: Known mitochondrial disorders caused by POLG mutations (BLACK BOX WARNING)
interactions: Enzyme inhibitor: increases levels of lamotrigine (risk of SJS), phenytoin, phenobarbital, and warfarin.
Carbapenems (e.g., meropenem) can significantly decrease valproate levels, leading to loss of seizure control.
Aspirin can increase free valproate levels.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic, via glucuronidation and mitochondrial beta-oxidation.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Renal excretion of metabolites.

Valproic Acid / Divalproex Sodium.clinicalNotes: Broad-spectrum antiepileptic used for focal, generalized (absence, myoclonic, tonic-clonic) seizures. Also indicated for bipolar disorder (mania) and migraine prophylaxis. Requires regular monitoring of LFTs, CBC (especially platelets), and serum ammonia levels. Therapeutic drug monitoring is essential. Divalproex sodium is an enteric-coated formulation that may have better GI tolerability.
Valproic Acid / Divalproex Sodium.antidote: L-carnitine for valproate-induced hyperammonemia and suspected overdose.

valsartan.MOA: Selectively blocks the binding of angiotensin II to the AT1 receptor in tissues such as vascular smooth muscle and the adrenal gland. This inhibits the vasoconstrictive and aldosterone-secreting effects of angiotensin II, leading to vasodilation and a decrease in blood pressure. Unlike ACE inhibitors, it does not affect the response to bradykinin.
contraindications: Concomitant use with aliskiren in patients with diabetes mellitus
interactions: Potassium-sparing diuretics or potassium supplements (increased risk of hyperkalemia)
NSAIDs (may reduce antihypertensive effect and increase risk of renal impairment)
Dual RAAS blockade (with ACE inhibitors or aliskiren) increases risk of hypotension, hyperkalemia, and renal impairment
Lithium (may increase lithium levels and toxicity)

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Minimal hepatic metabolism, minor contribution from CYP2C9.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily excreted as unchanged drug in feces (via biliary excretion) and urine.

valsartan.clinicalNotes: Used for hypertension, heart failure, and post-myocardial infarction in patients with left ventricular dysfunction. ARBs are often used as an alternative for patients who cannot tolerate ACE inhibitors due to cough. Monitor renal function and potassium levels, especially at initiation and with dose changes.
valsartan.antidote: No specific antidote. Treatment is supportive. For overdose-induced hypotension, place patient in supine position and administer IV normal saline. Vasopressors may be used if needed.

vancomycin.MOA: Inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors, preventing transglycosylation and transpeptidation, leading to cell lysis.
ADEs: Red man syndrome (rate-dependent infusion reaction due to histamine release)
contraindications: Allergy to corn or corn products (for IV formulations containing corn derivatives)
interactions: Increased risk of nephrotoxicity with other nephrotoxic agents (e.g., aminoglycosides, piperacillin-tazobactam, amphotericin B, loop diuretics, NSAIDs)
Increased risk of ototoxicity with other ototoxic agents (e.g., aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, cisplatin)

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Minimal metabolism.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily renal excretion as unchanged drug. Requires dose adjustment in renal impairment.

vancomycin.clinicalNotes: Primarily used for serious Gram-positive infections, including MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus). Oral formulation is not systemically absorbed and is used exclusively for the treatment of Clostridioides difficile colitis. Intravenous administration requires slow infusion (over at least 60 minutes) to prevent Red Man Syndrome. Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) of trough levels is essential to ensure efficacy and minimize toxicity (target trough typically 10-20 mcg/mL).
vancomycin.antidote: No specific antidote. Treatment is supportive. For Red Man Syndrome, stop or slow the infusion and administer antihistamines (e.g., diphenhydramine).

vardenafil.MOA: Inhibits phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5), an enzyme found primarily in the corpus cavernosum of the penis. This inhibition increases cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) levels, leading to smooth muscle relaxation and increased blood flow into the penis upon sexual stimulation, facilitating erection.
contraindications: Concurrent use of any form of organic nitrates (e.g., nitroglycerin)
Concurrent use of guanylate cyclase (GC) stimulators (e.g., riociguat)
Patients for whom sexual activity is inadvisable due to cardiovascular status
interactions: Nitrates and guanylate cyclase stimulators
Alpha-blockers (e.g., tamsulosin, doxazosin)
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, ritonavir)
Antihypertensives
Alcohol
QT-prolonging drugs (e.g., Class IA and III antiarrhythmics)

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Primarily hepatic, via CYP3A4 (major pathway) and CYP2C9 (minor pathway).
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Predominantly in feces as metabolites (approx. 95%), with a small amount in urine.

vardenafil.clinicalNotes: Used for the treatment of erectile dysfunction. Onset of action is approximately 25-60 minutes and requires sexual stimulation to be effective. Use with caution in patients with cardiovascular disease, anatomical penis deformation, or conditions predisposing to priapism. The orally disintegrating tablet (Staxyn) is not bioequivalent to the film-coated tablet (Levitra) on a mg-per-mg basis and should not be interchanged.
vardenafil.antidote: No specific antidote exists. Treatment for overdose is supportive. Priapism may be treated with aspiration and irrigation, or intracavernosal injection of a sympathomimetic agent like phenylephrine.

varenicline.MOA: Acts as a partial agonist at the α4β2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. This action both reduces cravings for nicotine and decreases the pleasurable effects of cigarettes and other tobacco products by blocking nicotine from binding to the receptor.
ADEs: Neuropsychiatric symptoms (e.g., agitation, depression, suicidal ideation)
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to varenicline or any component of the formulation.
interactions: Alcohol (may increase intoxicating effects)
Nicotine replacement therapy (increased incidence of adverse effects like nausea and headache)
Cimetidine (can increase varenicline levels by decreasing renal clearance)

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Minimal; less than 10% is metabolized.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily renal excretion ( >90% as unchanged drug). Requires dose adjustment in severe renal impairment.

varenicline.clinicalNotes: Initiate dosing one week before the patient's target quit date. The dose is titrated up to minimize nausea. Monitor for changes in mood and behavior. It has been shown to be more effective than bupropion or nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation.
varenicline.antidote: No specific antidote. Management is supportive.

Varicella Vaccine.MOA: Induces an active immune response by introducing a live, attenuated strain of the varicella-zoster virus (Oka/Merck strain), leading to the production of neutralizing antibodies and cell-mediated immunity against VZV.
contraindications: History of anaphylaxis to vaccine components (e.g., neomycin, gelatin)
Severe immunodeficiency (e.g., hematologic/solid tumors, congenital immunodeficiency, long-term immunosuppressive therapy, HIV with severe immunosuppression)
interactions: Immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., corticosteroids) may reduce vaccine efficacy and increase risk of disseminated infection.
Antibody-containing blood products (e.g., immunoglobulins) can interfere with the immune response; vaccination should be deferred.
Salicylates (Aspirin): Avoid for 6 weeks post-vaccination due to the theoretical risk of Reye's syndrome.
Other live vaccines: If not administered simultaneously, should be separated by at least 4 weeks.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Not applicable in the traditional sense. The attenuated virus replicates to a limited extent to induce an immune response.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Cleared by the host's immune system.

Varicella Vaccine.clinicalNotes: Administered as a 2-dose series, typically at 12-15 months and 4-6 years. Can be used for post-exposure prophylaxis if given within 3-5 days of exposure. Breakthrough infections can occur but are usually milder than natural varicella. There is a very low risk of transmission of the vaccine-strain virus from a vaccinated person with a rash to a susceptible contact.
Varicella Vaccine.antidote: Acyclovir may be used for disseminated vaccine-strain infection; Epinephrine for anaphylaxis.

vasopressin.MOA: Directly stimulates V1 (vascular smooth muscle) and V2 (renal tubule) receptors. V1 stimulation causes potent vasoconstriction, increasing systemic vascular resistance and mean arterial pressure. V2 stimulation increases water permeability in the renal collecting ducts, leading to decreased urine output and increased water reabsorption (antidiuresis).
contraindications: Vascular disease (especially coronary artery disease), when used for non-shock indications
interactions: Potentiated antidiuretic effect with carbamazepine, chlorpropamide, SSRIs.
Decreased antidiuretic effect with lithium, demeclocycline, norepinephrine.
Increased pressor effect with ganglionic blocking agents.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Rapidly metabolized in the liver and kidneys by vasopressinases.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Renal. Half-life is approximately 10-20 minutes.

vasopressin.clinicalNotes: Used in the treatment of central diabetes insipidus and vasodilatory shock (e.g., septic shock). It is a non-catecholamine vasopressor. Monitor fluid status, serum electrolytes (especially sodium), and signs of peripheral/end-organ ischemia closely. Its role in ACLS for cardiac arrest has been de-emphasized in recent guidelines.
vasopressin.antidote: No specific antidote. For water intoxication, implement fluid restriction and manage hyponatremia. For severe vasoconstriction/ischemia, discontinue the infusion and consider vasodilators.

vecuronium.MOA: Competitively antagonizes acetylcholine (ACh) at the nicotinic receptors on the motor endplate, preventing depolarization of the muscle cell membrane and leading to skeletal muscle paralysis.
contraindications: Inability to secure an airway and provide mechanical ventilation
interactions: Potentiation of effect by: inhaled anesthetics (e.g., sevoflurane), aminoglycosides, clindamycin, magnesium, loop diuretics.
Antagonism of effect by: chronic anticonvulsant therapy (phenytoin, carbamazepine), calcium.
Use of succinylcholine prior to vecuronium may enhance its effects.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Primarily hepatic, with active metabolites (3-desacetylvecuronium).
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily biliary/fecal excretion, with some renal excretion. Duration of action is prolonged in hepatic and renal impairment.

vecuronium.clinicalNotes: An intermediate-acting neuromuscular blocker used for skeletal muscle relaxation during surgery or mechanical ventilation. It has minimal cardiovascular effects as it lacks vagolytic properties and does not cause significant histamine release. Its effects can be reversed.
vecuronium.antidote: Sugammadex; Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., neostigmine) co-administered with an anticholinergic agent (e.g., glycopyrrolate).

velpatasvir.MOA: Inhibits the hepatitis C virus (HCV) non-structural protein 5A (NS5A), a phosphoprotein essential for viral RNA replication and virion assembly. This inhibition prevents the virus from multiplying.
ADEs: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) reactivation (black box warning when used in combination regimens)
contraindications: Coadministration with strong P-gp inducers and/or strong CYP inducers (e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's wort) which may lead to reduced therapeutic effect.
When used in combination with ribavirin, all contraindications to ribavirin apply (e.g., pregnancy).
interactions: Amiodarone: Can cause serious symptomatic bradycardia when used with sofosbuvir-containing regimens.

Acid-reducing agents (PPIs, H2-receptor antagonists, antacids): Can decrease velpatasvir absorption and plasma concentration. Administration must be separated or is not recommended with certain regimens.
Strong P-gp/CYP inducers (e.g., rifampin, St. John's wort): Significantly decrease velpatasvir levels, reducing efficacy. Coadministration is contraindicated.
Statins (e.g., rosuvastatin): May increase statin concentrations, increasing the risk of myopathy.
Digoxin: May increase digoxin concentrations; therapeutic monitoring is recommended.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Substrate of CYP2B6, CYP2C8, and CYP3A4. Metabolism is a minor clearance pathway.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily via feces as unchanged drug (>90%); minimal renal elimination.

velpatasvir.clinicalNotes: Velpatasvir is a pangenotypic HCV inhibitor, effective against all 6 major HCV genotypes. It is always used in a fixed-dose combination, most commonly with sofosbuvir (e.g., Epclusa®) or with sofosbuvir and voxilaprevir (e.g., Vosevi®). All patients should be tested for evidence of current or prior HBV infection before initiating treatment due to the risk of HBV reactivation.

venetoclax.MOA: Selectively inhibits B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2), an anti-apoptotic protein. By binding to BCL-2, venetoclax restores the normal apoptotic process, allowing pro-apoptotic proteins to initiate programmed cell death (apoptosis) in malignant cells that overexpress BCL-2.
contraindications: Concomitant use with strong CYP3A inhibitors during the initiation and dose ramp-up phase due to increased risk of Tumor Lysis Syndrome.
interactions: Strong and moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, clarithromycin, diltiazem, grapefruit juice) increase venetoclax levels and risk of toxicity.
Strong and moderate CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine, St. John's wort) decrease venetoclax levels and efficacy.
P-glycoprotein (P-gp) inhibitors (e.g., amiodarone, cyclosporine) may increase venetoclax concentrations.
Warfarin (monitor INR closely).

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Primarily hepatic via CYP3A4.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily in feces (>99%), with minimal renal excretion.

venetoclax.clinicalNotes: A critical risk is Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS), especially upon initiation. Requires a gradual 5-week dose ramp-up schedule. Patient risk for TLS must be assessed before starting therapy to guide prophylaxis (hydration, antihyperuricemics like allopurinol or rasburicase) and monitoring. Indicated for Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL), Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL), and Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML).
venetoclax.antidote: No specific antidote. Management is supportive.

venlafaxine.MOA: Potent inhibitor of neuronal serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake and a weak inhibitor of dopamine reuptake. At lower doses (<150 mg/day), it acts primarily as a serotonin reuptake inhibitor. At higher doses, norepinephrine reuptake inhibition becomes more significant.
ADEs: Discontinuation syndrome (prominent due to short half-life, requires slow taper)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to venlafaxine or any component
Concurrent use with or within 14 days of discontinuing Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs)
Initiation in patients being treated with linezolid or intravenous methylene blue
interactions: MAOIs: Increased risk of serotonin syndrome; requires a 14-day washout period.
Other serotonergic agents (SSRIs, triptans, tramadol, St. John's wort): Increased risk of serotonin syndrome.
Antiplatelet agents and anticoagulants (NSAIDs, aspirin, warfarin): Increased risk of bleeding.
CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 inhibitors: May increase venlafaxine concentrations.
Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs): May increase TCA levels and risk of toxicity.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively hepatic, primarily via CYP2D6 to its major active metabolite, O-desmethylvenlafaxine (ODV).
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily renal, as metabolites and a small amount of unchanged drug. Short half-life (venlafaxine ~5 hrs, ODV ~11 hrs).

venlafaxine.clinicalNotes: Used for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), Social Anxiety Disorder, and Panic Disorder. Monitor blood pressure at baseline and with dose increases. Abrupt discontinuation can cause a severe withdrawal syndrome ('brain zaps', dizziness, nausea); a gradual taper is necessary. The extended-release (XR) formulation is generally preferred for better tolerability and once-daily dosing.
venlafaxine.antidote: No specific antidote. Treatment is supportive. For severe serotonin syndrome, cyproheptadine may be administered.

verapamil.MOA: Inhibits voltage-dependent L-type calcium channels in cardiac muscle, SA/AV nodes, and vascular smooth muscle. This results in decreased myocardial contractility (negative inotropy), decreased heart rate (negative chronotropy), and slowed AV conduction (negative dromotropy). It also causes arterial vasodilation, reducing systemic vascular resistance.
contraindications: Severe left ventricular dysfunction (e.g., decompensated heart failure)
Sick sinus syndrome (unless a permanent pacemaker is in place)
Second or third-degree AV block (unless a permanent pacemaker is in place)
Atrial fibrillation/flutter with an accessory bypass tract (e.g., Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome)
interactions: Beta-blockers (additive effects on heart rate, AV conduction, and contractility, increasing risk of bradycardia and heart failure)
Digoxin (verapamil increases digoxin levels)
CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., grapefruit juice, macrolides) increase verapamil levels
CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin, St. John's Wort) decrease verapamil levels
Statins (e.g., simvastatin, lovastatin) - verapamil increases statin levels, raising risk of myopathy

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Liver, extensively by CYP3A4. Subject to significant first-pass metabolism.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily renal as metabolites.

verapamil.clinicalNotes: Used to manage hypertension, angina, and supraventricular arrhythmias (e.g., rate control in atrial fibrillation). Unlike dihydropyridines (e.g., amlodipine), it has significant cardiac effects. Constipation is a very common and often dose-limiting side effect.
verapamil.antidote: Intravenous calcium gluconate or calcium chloride, glucagon, atropine for bradycardia, vasopressors for hypotension.

Verapamil.MOA: Inhibits voltage-dependent calcium channels (L-type) in vascular smooth muscle and myocardium. This leads to coronary and peripheral vasodilation (decreased afterload), decreased myocardial contractility (negative inotropy), and slowed AV nodal conduction (negative dromotropy).
contraindications: Severe left ventricular dysfunction (e.g., decompensated heart failure)
Sick sinus syndrome (unless pacemaker is present)
Second- or third-degree AV block (unless pacemaker is present)
Atrial fibrillation/flutter with an accessory bypass tract (e.g., Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome)
interactions: Beta-blockers (additive negative inotropic and chronotropic effects, increasing risk of bradycardia and heart failure)
Digoxin (verapamil increases digoxin levels)
CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., grapefruit juice, clarithromycin) can increase verapamil levels
CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin) can decrease verapamil levels
Statins (e.g., simvastatin); verapamil increases statin levels, raising risk of myopathy

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver by CYP3A4. Its major active metabolite is norverapamil.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily renal excretion of metabolites.

Verapamil.clinicalNotes: Used for hypertension, angina, and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias (e.g., atrial fibrillation rate control). Unlike dihydropyridine CCBs, it has significant effects on the myocardium (contractility) and AV node (conduction). Constipation is a very common and often dose-limiting side effect.
Verapamil.antidote: Calcium gluconate or calcium chloride; glucagon; atropine (for bradycardia); vasopressors.

vilanterol.MOA: Selectively stimulates beta2-adrenergic receptors in the lungs, leading to relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle and bronchodilation. It achieves this by activating adenylyl cyclase, which increases intracellular levels of cyclic AMP (cAMP).
ADEs: Increased risk of asthma-related death when used as monotherapy
contraindications: Status asthmaticus or other acute episodes of asthma or COPD
Severe hypersensitivity to milk proteins (for dry powder formulations)
Monotherapy for the treatment of asthma
interactions: Beta-blockers (may block bronchodilatory effects)
MAO inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressants (may potentiate cardiovascular effects)
Non-potassium-sparing diuretics (may worsen hypokalemia/ECG changes)
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, ritonavir) may increase vilanterol exposure

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic, primarily by CYP3A4.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily via metabolites in urine and feces; terminal half-life is approximately 11-21 hours.

vilanterol.clinicalNotes: Vilanterol is an ultra-LABA with a 24-hour duration of action, allowing for once-daily dosing. It is only available in combination products (e.g., with fluticasone furoate or umeclidinium) for the maintenance treatment of COPD and asthma. It is not indicated for the relief of acute bronchospasm. A boxed warning exists for all LABAs regarding the increased risk of asthma-related death when used as monotherapy.
vilanterol.antidote: No specific antidote. A cardioselective beta-blocker may be considered in severe overdose but must be used with extreme caution in patients with bronchospastic disease.

vilazodone.MOA: Dual mechanism of action: selectively inhibits the reuptake of serotonin (5-HT), increasing its concentration in the synaptic cleft, and acts as a partial agonist at the 5-HT1A receptor.
contraindications: Concurrent use with or within 14 days of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)
interactions: MAOIs (increased risk of serotonin syndrome)
Other serotonergic drugs (e.g., SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, tramadol, St. John's wort) increase risk of serotonin syndrome
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, clarithromycin) may increase vilazodone levels
Strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., carbamazepine, rifampin) may decrease vilazodone levels

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic, primarily via CYP3A4, with minor contributions from CYP2C19 and CYP2D6.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily renal and fecal. Half-life is approximately 25 hours.

vilazodone.clinicalNotes: Indicated for the treatment of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). Must be taken with food to ensure adequate absorption. Gradual dose titration is recommended to minimize gastrointestinal side effects. Carries a black box warning for increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults.
vilazodone.antidote: No specific antidote exists. Treatment is supportive. For serotonin syndrome, discontinuation of the offending agent and supportive care are primary; cyproheptadine (a serotonin antagonist) may be considered in moderate to severe cases.

vinblastine.MOA: Binds to tubulin and inhibits microtubule polymerization, disrupting the assembly of the mitotic spindle. This arrests the cell in the M-phase (metaphase) of the cell cycle, leading to apoptosis.
contraindications: Significant granulocytopenia (unless due to the disease being treated)
interactions: CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, ritonavir) increase toxicity
CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., phenytoin, rifampin) decrease efficacy
Concomitant use with other myelosuppressive agents enhances hematologic toxicity
Live vaccines (contraindicated due to immunosuppression)
May decrease plasma concentrations of phenytoin

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively hepatic, primarily via CYP3A4.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily through biliary excretion into feces; minor renal excretion.

vinblastine.clinicalNotes: FATAL if administered intrathecally. It is a potent vesicant and must be administered carefully via a free-flowing IV line. Myelosuppression, particularly neutropenia, is the dose-limiting toxicity. A key component of the ABVD regimen for Hodgkin's lymphoma. Compared to vincristine, vinblastine has more myelosuppression but less neurotoxicity.
vinblastine.antidote: For extravasation: apply warm compresses and inject hyaluronidase subcutaneously around the site. No systemic antidote for overdose; treatment is supportive.

vincristine.MOA: Binds to tubulin dimers, inhibiting their polymerization into microtubules. This disrupts the formation of the mitotic spindle, arresting cells in the M-phase (metaphase) and leading to apoptosis.
ADEs: Peripheral neuropathy (dose-limiting, often manifests as paresthesias, loss of deep tendon reflexes, foot drop)
Myelosuppression (typically mild compared to other vinca alkaloids)
SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone secretion)
Vesicant (causes severe tissue damage if extravasation occurs)
contraindications: Patients with the demyelinating form of Charcot-Marie-Tooth syndrome
interactions: CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., azole antifungals, protease inhibitors) may increase vincristine levels and neurotoxicity.
CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., phenytoin, carbamazepine) may decrease vincristine levels.
Concurrent use with other neurotoxic agents can potentiate neurotoxicity.
May decrease the therapeutic effect of live vaccines and increase the risk of infection.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively metabolized by the liver, primarily via the CYP3A4 enzyme system.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily through the biliary system and excreted in the feces; a smaller amount is excreted in the urine.

vincristine.clinicalNotes: BLACK BOX WARNING: For intravenous use only. Fatal if given intrathecally. To prevent accidental intrathecal administration, vincristine should be prepared in a small volume IV bag (minibag) rather than a syringe. Doses are often capped at 2 mg in adults to limit neurotoxicity. A key component of many combination chemotherapy regimens, such as CHOP for non-Hodgkin lymphoma and VAMP for ALL.
vincristine.antidote: No specific systemic antidote. For extravasation, apply moderate heat (warm compresses) and administer hyaluronidase locally to enhance systemic absorption of the drug from the tissue.

Vitamins.MOA: Act as essential cofactors, coenzymes, antioxidants, and signaling molecules in numerous metabolic pathways. They are crucial for cell growth, differentiation, and function. Each vitamin has a specific mechanism.
ADEs: Hypervitaminosis (especially with fat-soluble vitamins A and D, leading to toxicity)
Specific toxicities related to individual vitamins (e.g., flushing with niacin, neuropathy with high-dose pyridoxine, kidney stones with high-dose vitamin C)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to any component of the preparation
Pre-existing hypervitaminosis for a specific vitamin
interactions: Vitamin K antagonizes the effect of warfarin.
High-dose Vitamin E can potentiate anticoagulant effects.
Certain medications can impair vitamin absorption (e.g., orlistat, mineral oil for fat-soluble vitamins; metformin for vitamin B12).
Pyridoxine (B6) can decrease the efficacy of levodopa.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Varies significantly by vitamin. Fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the liver and adipose tissue. Water-soluble vitamins are generally not stored in large amounts (exception: B12 in the liver).
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Water-soluble vitamins and their metabolites are primarily excreted in the urine. Fat-soluble vitamins are eliminated more slowly, primarily through feces via biliary excretion.

Vitamins.clinicalNotes: Vitamins are classified into two groups: Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) which are absorbed with lipids and can accumulate in the body, posing a risk for toxicity. Water-soluble (B-complex and C) which are not stored in significant amounts (except B12) and excess is typically excreted in the urine. Deficiencies lead to specific diseases (e.g., scurvy from Vitamin C deficiency, rickets from Vitamin D deficiency, pellagra from Niacin [B3] deficiency, megaloblastic anemia from B12/Folate deficiency).
Vitamins.antidote: No specific universal antidote. Management of toxicity involves discontinuation of the supplement and supportive care.
ingredients: Vitamin B complex (Thiamine, Riboflavin, Niacin, Pantothenic acid, Pyridoxine, Biotin, Folate, Cobalamin)

voriconazole.MOA: Inhibits fungal cytochrome P450-dependent enzyme lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, which is essential for the synthesis of ergosterol, a key component of the fungal cell membrane. This disrupts membrane structure and function, leading to inhibition of fungal growth.
ADEs: Visual disturbances (blurred vision, color changes, photophobia)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to voriconazole or other azoles
Coadministration with potent CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine, St. John's wort)
Coadministration with certain CYP3A4 substrates that prolong the QTc interval (e.g., cisapride, quinidine, pimozide)
interactions: Potent inhibitor of CYP2C19, CYP2C9, and CYP3A4, increasing levels of many drugs (e.g., cyclosporine, tacrolimus, warfarin, statins, sulfonylureas).
Its own metabolism is affected by CYP inducers (e.g., rifampin, phenytoin), which decrease voriconazole levels, and inhibitors.
Exhibits non-linear pharmacokinetics, making interactions difficult to predict.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively hepatic, primarily by CYP2C19, and to a lesser extent by CYP2C9 and CYP3A4. Subject to genetic polymorphism in CYP2C19, leading to variable drug levels.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily renal excretion of inactive metabolites; less than 2% of the dose is excreted as unchanged drug.

voriconazole.clinicalNotes: Drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis. Also used for candidemia and other serious fungal infections. Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is recommended to ensure efficacy and minimize toxicity. The IV formulation contains a cyclodextrin vehicle (SBECD) which accumulates in renal insufficiency (CrCl <50 mL/min); oral formulation is preferred in these patients.
voriconazole.antidote: No specific antidote. Treatment is supportive.

vortioxetine.MOA: Inhibits reuptake of serotonin (5-HT). Additionally, it acts as an agonist at 5-HT1A receptors, a partial agonist at 5-HT1B receptors, and an antagonist at 5-HT3, 5-HT1D, and 5-HT7 receptors, leading to modulation of serotonergic neurotransmission.
ADEs: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors (black box warning)
contraindications: Concomitant use with or within 14 days of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)
interactions: MAOIs (increased risk of serotonin syndrome)
Other serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, tramadol, St. John's Wort)
Drugs that impair hemostasis (NSAIDs, aspirin, warfarin)
Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (e.g., bupropion, fluoxetine) may increase vortioxetine levels
Strong CYP inducers (e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine) may decrease vortioxetine levels

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively hepatic, primarily via CYP2D6 to an inactive major metabolite.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily in urine as metabolites; long half-life of approximately 66 hours.

vortioxetine.clinicalNotes: Used for the treatment of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). The multimodal mechanism may offer benefits for cognitive symptoms associated with depression. Nausea is a very common dose-dependent side effect, often transient, and can be minimized by taking with food. Discontinuation should be tapered to avoid withdrawal symptoms.
vortioxetine.antidote: No specific antidote. Treatment is supportive. For serotonin syndrome, cyproheptadine may be used.

warfarin.MOA: Inhibits the vitamin K-dependent synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as regulatory proteins C and S, by inhibiting the enzyme Vitamin K Epoxide Reductase Complex 1 (VKORC1).
contraindications: Recent or potential major surgery (especially CNS or eye)
High risk of falls or non-compliance
interactions: CYP2C9 inhibitors (e.g., amiodarone, fluconazole, metronidazole, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole) increase INR
CYP2C9 inducers (e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital) decrease INR
Antibiotics altering gut flora (decrease Vitamin K production, increase INR)
Drugs affecting platelet function (e.g., NSAIDs, aspirin, clopidogrel) increase bleeding risk without changing INR
High Vitamin K-containing foods (e.g., leafy greens) decrease INR
Acetaminophen (>2g/day) may increase INR

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic, primarily via CYP2C9. Genetic polymorphisms in CYP2C9 and VKORC1 influence dose requirements.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Renal, as inactive metabolites.

warfarin.clinicalNotes: Requires routine monitoring with International Normalized Ratio (INR); therapeutic range is typically 2.0-3.0. Has a narrow therapeutic index and delayed onset of action (3-5 days). Bridging with a parenteral anticoagulant is often necessary at initiation for acute thrombosis. Patient education regarding diet, drug interactions, and signs of bleeding is critical.
warfarin.antidote: Vitamin K (phytonadione). For urgent reversal of major bleeding, Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC) or Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) is used.

Yellow (Flavoxantine).MOA: Agonist at melatonergic MT1 and MT2 receptors, which helps re-synchronize circadian rhythms. It is also an antagonist at serotonin 5-HT2C receptors, which disinhibits and thereby increases norepinephrine and dopamine release in the frontal cortex.
contraindications: Concomitant use with strong CYP1A2 inhibitors (e.g., fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin)
interactions: Strong CYP1A2 inhibitors (e.g., fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin) significantly increase drug exposure.
CYP1A2 inducers (e.g., smoking, rifampin) decrease drug exposure.
Alcohol and other CNS depressants cause additive sedative effects.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic, extensive first-pass metabolism primarily via CYP1A2.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Renal, as inactive metabolites. Short half-life (1-3 hours).

Yellow (Flavoxantine).clinicalNotes: Indicated for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), especially useful in patients with significant sleep disturbances. Has a favorable side effect profile regarding sexual dysfunction and weight gain compared to SSRIs. Requires administration at bedtime due to sedative properties. **BLACK BOX WARNING**: Potential for hepatotoxicity; liver function tests (LFTs) must be monitored at baseline, after dose initiation/titration, and periodically thereafter. Discontinue if LFTs exceed 3x the upper limit of normal.
Yellow (Flavoxantine).antidote: None. Treatment is supportive and symptomatic.

zafirlukast.MOA: Selectively and competitively blocks the cysteinyl leukotriene 1 (CysLT1) receptor, inhibiting the effects of leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4). This reduces airway edema, smooth muscle constriction, and inflammation associated with asthma.
ADEs: Neuropsychiatric events (e.g., depression, agitation, sleep disturbances)
interactions: Warfarin (increases prothrombin time)
Theophylline (decreases zafirlukast levels)
Erythromycin (decreases zafirlukast levels)
Aspirin (increases zafirlukast levels)
CYP2C9 inhibitors (e.g., fluconazole) may increase zafirlukast levels
CYP2C9 inducers (e.g., phenytoin, carbamazepine) may decrease zafirlukast levels

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively hepatic, primarily via CYP2C9.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily fecal (~90%) with a small amount in urine (~10%) as metabolites.

zafirlukast.clinicalNotes: Used for prophylaxis and chronic treatment of asthma in patients 5 years and older. It is not a bronchodilator and should not be used to treat an acute asthma attack. Administration with food significantly reduces bioavailability; therefore, it should be taken at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals. Monitor LFTs periodically.
zafirlukast.antidote: No specific antidote. Treatment is supportive.

zaleplon.MOA: Selectively binds to the benzodiazepine type-1 (BZ1) receptor subunit on the GABA-A receptor complex, potentiating the inhibitory effects of GABA. This results in increased chloride ion conductance, hyperpolarization of the neuronal membrane, and CNS depression, primarily inducing sleep.
contraindications: History of complex sleep behaviors after taking zaleplon
interactions: CNS depressants (e.g., alcohol, opioids, other benzodiazepines) - additive CNS depression
CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, erythromycin) - may increase zaleplon levels
CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine) - may decrease zaleplon levels
Cimetidine - may increase zaleplon levels

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Primarily hepatic via aldehyde oxidase to inactive metabolites. Minor pathway via CYP3A4.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily renal as inactive metabolites. Very short half-life of approximately 1 hour.

zaleplon.clinicalNotes: Has a very rapid onset and short duration of action, making it useful for difficulty with sleep initiation. Can be taken for middle-of-the-night awakenings if at least 4 hours of sleep time remain. Less likely to cause next-day somnolence compared to other hypnotics due to its ultra-short half-life. It is a Schedule IV controlled substance.

zanamivir.MOA: Inhibits influenza virus neuraminidase, an enzyme that allows the release of newly formed virus particles from infected cells. Inhibition prevents viral budding and the spread of the virus to other cells.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to zanamivir or any component (e.g., lactose/milk proteins)
Not recommended for patients with underlying airway disease (e.g., asthma, COPD) due to risk of serious bronchospasm
interactions: Live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV): May inhibit viral replication of the vaccine. Avoid zanamivir 48 hours before and 2 weeks after LAIV administration.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Not metabolized. Acts locally in the respiratory tract.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: The small portion that is systemically absorbed is excreted unchanged in the urine.

zanamivir.clinicalNotes: Administered via oral inhalation using a specific device (Diskhaler). Used for treatment and prophylaxis of influenza A and B. Treatment must be initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset for maximal benefit. Not a substitute for annual influenza vaccination.
zanamivir.antidote: No specific antidote. Treatment is supportive.

zidovudine.MOA: A thymidine analogue that is phosphorylated to its active triphosphate form. It competes with deoxythymidine triphosphate for incorporation into viral DNA, inhibiting HIV-1 reverse transcriptase and causing viral DNA chain termination.
contraindications: Pre-existing severe bone marrow suppression (neutrophil count <750 cells/mm³ or hemoglobin <7.5 g/dL)
interactions: Myelosuppressive agents (e.g., ganciclovir, interferon-alpha) increase risk of hematologic toxicity.
Stavudine (antagonistic effect; co-administration is contraindicated).
Probenecid (increases zidovudine levels).
Rifampin (may decrease zidovudine levels).

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic via glucuronidation.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Renal, primarily as the glucuronide metabolite.

zidovudine.clinicalNotes: First antiretroviral drug approved for HIV. Its use has decreased due to toxicity, but it remains a key component of regimens for preventing perinatal HIV transmission. Regular monitoring of complete blood count (CBC) is essential due to the high risk of bone marrow suppression.
zidovudine.antidote: No specific antidote. Management is supportive care and discontinuation of the drug if severe toxicity occurs.

zileuton.MOA: Selectively inhibits 5-lipoxygenase, the enzyme that catalyzes the formation of leukotrienes (LTB4, LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4) from arachidonic acid. By blocking leukotriene synthesis, it reduces inflammation, edema, mucus secretion, and bronchoconstriction in the airways.
ADEs: Neuropsychiatric events (e.g., sleep disorders, behavioral changes)
contraindications: Persistent elevations of serum transaminases (≥3 times the upper limit of normal)
interactions: Increases plasma concentrations of theophylline, warfarin, and propranolol (CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 inhibitor). Dose reduction of these agents may be required.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic, via CYP1A2, 2C9, and 3A4, and glucuronidation.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Renal (as metabolites)

zileuton.clinicalNotes: Used for the prophylaxis and chronic treatment of asthma in adults and children 12 years and older. Not indicated for acute bronchospasm. Liver function (ALT) must be monitored before initiation, once a month for the first 3 months, every 2-3 months for the remainder of the first year, and periodically thereafter. The immediate-release formulation is taken four times daily, which can affect compliance.
zileuton.antidote: No specific antidote. Treatment is supportive.

ziprasidone.MOA: Acts as an antagonist at dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. It also possesses antagonistic activity at alpha-1 adrenergic and H1 histaminergic receptors, and agonistic activity at 5-HT1A receptors. It inhibits the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine.
ADEs: Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS)
contraindications: History of QTc prolongation, congenital long QT syndrome
Concurrent use with other drugs known to prolong the QT interval (e.g., Class IA and III antiarrhythmics, certain antipsychotics, antibiotics)
interactions: QTc-prolonging drugs (additive effect, contraindicated)
CNS depressants (e.g., alcohol, benzodiazepines) may enhance sedative effects
CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole) can increase ziprasidone levels
CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., carbamazepine) can decrease ziprasidone levels
Antihypertensive agents (may enhance hypotensive effects)

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively hepatic, primarily via aldehyde oxidase and to a lesser extent by CYP3A4.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily via feces (~66%) and urine (~20%) as metabolites.

ziprasidone.clinicalNotes: Administration must be with food (at least 500 calories) to ensure adequate absorption, which can increase up to twofold. Carries a significant risk of dose-related QTc prolongation, requiring baseline and periodic ECG monitoring, especially in at-risk patients. Black Box Warning: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis.
ziprasidone.antidote: No specific antidote exists. Treatment is supportive and symptomatic, with close monitoring of cardiac function (ECG) due to the risk of QTc prolongation and arrhythmias.

zolmitriptan.MOA: Selective agonist for serotonin (5-HT) receptors 1B and 1D located on intracranial blood vessels and sensory nerves of the trigeminal system. This results in cranial vessel vasoconstriction, inhibition of neuropeptide release (e.g., CGRP), and reduced transmission in trigeminal pain pathways.
contraindications: Ischemic heart disease (e.g., myocardial infarction, angina pectoris)
history of stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA)
use within 2 weeks of MAO-A inhibitors
use within 24 hours of another 5-HT1 agonist or ergot-type medication
interactions: MAO-A inhibitors (increase zolmitriptan levels; contraindicated)
Ergot-containing medications (additive vasospastic effects; contraindicated within 24 hours)
Other 5-HT1 agonists (e.g., other triptans; additive effects; contraindicated within 24 hours)
SSRIs/SNRIs (increased risk of serotonin syndrome; use with caution)
Cimetidine (inhibits metabolism, increasing zolmitriptan levels)

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic, primarily via CYP1A2 and MAO-A, to an active N-desmethyl metabolite and inactive metabolites.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily renal excretion of metabolites and unchanged drug.

zolmitriptan.clinicalNotes: Used for acute treatment of migraine with or without aura, not for prophylaxis. The first dose should be administered at the onset of a migraine. A second dose can be taken after 2 hours if the headache returns or does not resolve. Available as oral tablets, orally disintegrating tablets, and a nasal spray.
zolmitriptan.antidote: No specific antidote exists. Treatment is supportive.

zolpidem.MOA: Selectively binds to the alpha-1 subunit of the GABA-A receptor complex, enhancing the inhibitory effects of GABA. This differs from benzodiazepines which bind non-selectively to multiple alpha subunits.
contraindications: History of complex sleep behaviors after taking zolpidem
interactions: Additive CNS depression with alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and other CNS depressants
CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, itraconazole) increase zolpidem levels
CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin, St. John's wort) decrease zolpidem levels

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic, primarily via CYP3A4
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Renal, as inactive metabolites; short half-life (~2.5 hours)

zolpidem.clinicalNotes: Used for the short-term treatment of insomnia. It is a Schedule IV controlled substance. Lower doses are recommended for women and elderly patients due to decreased clearance and increased risk of next-day impairment. Available in immediate-release, extended-release, and sublingual formulations.

zonisamide.MOA: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and T-type calcium channels, leading to stabilization of neuronal membranes. Also a weak inhibitor of carbonic anhydrase and may modulate GABAergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission.
interactions: CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., carbamazepine, phenytoin) decrease zonisamide levels
CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole) increase zonisamide levels
Other carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., topiramate) increase risk of metabolic acidosis and nephrolithiasis
Additive CNS depression with other sedatives (e.g., alcohol, benzodiazepines)

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic, primarily via CYP3A4.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Primarily renal, as both unchanged drug and metabolites; has a long half-life (~63 hours).

zonisamide.clinicalNotes: Used as adjunctive therapy for partial-onset seizures. Due to its sulfonamide structure, there is a risk of serious skin reactions (SJS/TEN) and cross-reactivity in patients with sulfa allergies. Monitor for metabolic acidosis, nephrolithiasis, and oligohidrosis (decreased sweating), which can lead to hyperthermia, especially in children. Titrate slowly to minimize CNS side effects like cognitive impairment and somnolence.
zonisamide.antidote: No specific antidote. Treatment is supportive.

Zoster Vaccine, Recombinant (RZV).MOA: Contains a specific VZV surface antigen, glycoprotein E (gE), combined with an adjuvant (AS01B). This stimulates a strong and durable antigen-specific T-cell mediated immune response against the varicella-zoster virus, preventing its reactivation from latency, which causes herpes zoster (shingles).
ADEs: Injection site pain, redness, and swelling
contraindications: History of severe allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis) to any component of the vaccine or after a previous dose.
interactions: Immunosuppressive therapies (e.g., high-dose corticosteroids, chemotherapy) may reduce the immune response to the vaccine.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Not applicable. The vaccine components are processed locally by the immune system.
pharmacokinetics.elimination: Not applicable.

Zoster Vaccine, Recombinant (RZV).clinicalNotes: Brand name is Shingrix. Recommended by the ACIP for immunocompetent adults aged 50 years and older, and for adults ≥19 years who are or will be immunodeficient or immunosuppressed. Administered as a two-dose intramuscular series (0 and 2-6 months). It is the preferred vaccine over the previously available live-attenuated zoster vaccine (Zostavax), which is no longer distributed in the US.
Zoster Vaccine, Recombinant (RZV).antidote: Not applicable. Anaphylaxis is treated with epinephrine.
